notable_claims: Student premises and possessions should not be searched without appropriate authorization except in extreme emergencies.
Students should be present during searches of institution-controlled premises if possible.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie shares an excerpt from the 1977 AAUP Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students regarding the investigation of student conduct. The text outlines requirements for authorization and notification before searching premises or personal possessions occupied by students.
classification.title: Ethics of "Peeking;" requirement to notify subject

notable_claims: Disk space and e-mail should be treated similarly to assigned office space regarding privacy rights.
Government institutions cannot ignore Fourth Amendment protections simply because they own the facilities.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues that university rules regarding assigned office space should serve as a model for the treatment of disk space and email. He cites University of Illinois privacy policies and the Fourth Amendment to argue against warrantless searches of digital assets by government institutions.
classification.title: Ethics of "Peeking;" requirement to notify subject

classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie shared a notification regarding proposed legislation concerning the searching of computers. The item serves as an alert to the community about potential legal changes affecting digital privacy and access.
classification.title: FYI: Proposed law on computer searches

identity.subject: FYI: Proposed law on computer searches

notable_claims: Search warrants for electronic material are fundamentally different from search warrants for physical objects.
The proposal aims to prevent seized digital evidence from disappearing into a 'maw' of indefinite retention without progress reports.
Aligning state regulations with the federal Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA) and Privacy Protection Act reduces legal inconsistency and civil rights litigation.
classification.summary: Donald G. Ingraham, an Assistant District Attorney, proposed a draft amendment to the California Penal Code (Section 1538.6) to regulate the seizure and analysis of electronically stored material. The proposal sought to align state law with federal privacy acts while establishing strict requirements for inventorying seized data and providing standing for affected parties to petition for the return of materials. It emphasizes balancing law enforcement needs with the protection of private communications and business operations.
classification.title: Proposed law on computer searches

notable_claims: The 'magnus' system is intended for email and news, with accounts available to any university associate who agrees to policies.
Restrictive policies at OSU are attributed to the need to provide fair service across a potentially massive user base (up to 60,000) with limited resources.
System administrators often act as buffers between users and university bureaucracy to protect access privileges.
classification.summary: Mark Verber defends the Academic Computing Services (ACS) at Ohio State University against criticisms regarding restrictive network policies. He argues that restrictions on systems like 'magnus' are due to limited resources rather than malice and highlights the role of system administrators in defending user privileges from bureaucracy.

notable_claims: The Ohio State University ACS policy lacks explicit due process protections for users facing access denial.
University computer policies should be developed with the participation of the academic community and consistent with general university standards.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie critiques the 'Policy on Abuse of Computers and Networks' issued by The Ohio State University's Office of Academic Computing. He argues that the policy lacks due process protections and fails to define 'unreasonable' use or provide a clear appeals process for users denied access. To support his critique, he cites the Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students regarding procedural standards in disciplinary proceedings.
classification.title: Re: Ohio State ACS policy

notable_claims: The user's account was disabled without notice after a disagreement with the system administrator's boss regarding 'word processing' on a Unix machine.
Administrative discomfort with the merge of communication and computing contributed to the loss of access.
classification.summary: A student at Hamline University reports the sudden disabling of their Unix account after questioning a supervisor about printing services. The author suggests the account was terminated because administration was uncomfortable with non-mainframe computer usage and Internet access. This led to the student's eventual withdrawal from the university.
classification.title: Hamline Univ shuts off account w/o notice or stated reason
